headline: Scientists Unlock New Oxygen Chemistry Using a Molecular Basket
meta_description: Rice University chemists create unprecedented bonds between neodymium and oxygen using specially designed molecular structures, opening doors to new synthetic…
summary_short: Rice chemists have engineered a breakthrough allowing rare-earth metals to bond with oxygen in ways previously thought impossible, potentially replacing iron-based compo…
body:
Chemists at Rice University have achieved something the scientific community thought unlikely: they've engineered neodymium, a rare-earth metal, to form pi interactions with oxygen—bonds that were long considered impossible for this class of metals. Using a specially designed molecular structure they describe as a "basket," assistant professor Raúl Hernández Sánchez and his team positioned the atoms just right, enabling them to create highly reactive compounds called lanthanide oxos that could eventually replace iron-based molecules in both biological research and chemical manufacturing.

The breakthrough matters because iron oxos are everywhere in the human body. They're present in hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen through the bloodstream, and in liver enzymes that help break down drugs. By creating lanthanide oxo alternatives, chemists gain new tools for studying these essential biological reactions and developing synthetic alternatives when iron isn't ideal.

The "basket" itself is the key innovation—a ligand platform designed to hold a single lanthanide atom and position it precisely. The researchers arranged two molecular baskets opposite each other, connecting them with six atoms including a dioxygen molecule, creating what's called an octacoordinate ligand environment. This fine-tuned arrangement allowed neodymium and dioxygen to form the unexpected pi interactions that produced the reactive lanthanide oxo molecule. Though the published study focused solely on neodymium, Hernández Sánchez believes the same molecular scaffold could enable similar reactions with most lanthanides and probably actinides as well—potentially opening what he calls "a new chapter in the chemistry of lanthanides." The research was supported by Rice University startup funding and grants from the Robert A. Welch Foundation.
